courses.name: Personal & Professional Development

content.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
content.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
content.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
content.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.contribution: Firstyearacademic/reflective/civicformation
courses.selectedDescription: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

courses.name: Consumer Product Design

content.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
content.profile: Teaches consumer-product design and development through projects that progress from understanding an existing product to creating a new one. Students investigate product mechanisms and environmental impact, interview potential customers, translate needs into specifications, select concepts, and develop production plans and prototypes where feasible. The final project integrates these stages with industrial scaling and elementary economic analysis. Sustainability, including material use, repairability, lifespan and circularity, informs design decisions throughout.
content.topics: Consumer needs; Product concepts and specifications; Product working mechanisms; Prototyping; Laboratory-to-industrial production scaling; Materials and resource use; Product lifespan, repairability and circularity; Environmental impact; Production costs and commercial viability
content.methods: Consumer interviews; Needs ranking and specification development; Concept-criteria matrices; Quantitative product modelling; Product investigation and experimentation; Prototyping; Process-flow diagrams and material balances; Environmental-impact estimation; Break-even analysis

courses.contribution: develops customer-led product concepts, fabrication methods, prototypes, quantitative models and sustainability/cost analysis in a team design process
courses.selectedDescription: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.

courses.name: AI Ethics

content.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
content.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
content.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
content.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing

courses.contribution: examines interpretability, bias, alignment and responsibility in AI-enabled automated systems; it is not the external engineering-ethics unit
courses.selectedDescription: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

courses.name: Decision-making in AI

content.description2: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
content.profile: Develops the mathematical foundations of intelligent-agent decisions under uncertainty. Probability and Bayesian networks support belief updating and inference, while temporal models address changing environments. Decision theory, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems connect uncertainty to policies and expected utility. Multi-agent decisions introduce strategic and collective interaction, and probabilistic programming provides a framework for expressing models. Students work through equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.
content.topics: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' rule; Bayesian networks; Temporal probabilistic models; Hidden Markov models and dynamic Bayesian networks; Expected utility; Markov and partially observable decision processes; Exploration-exploitation trade-offs and bandits; Competitive and cooperative multi-agent interaction; Negotiation, auctions and voting; Probabilistic programming
content.methods: Probabilistic inference; Bayesian-network modelling; Temporal probabilistic modelling; Expected-utility analysis; Sequential decision modelling; Game-theoretic analysis; Probabilistic programming

courses.contribution: models planning under uncertainty, partial observability and resource constraints for intelligent systems
courses.selectedDescription: Decision-making in AI examines how intelligent agents make decisions under uncertainty. Students study probability, Bayesian networks, temporal models, expected utility, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems. Multi-agent decisions and probabilistic programming extend the analysis, supported by equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

courses.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics

content.description2: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
content.profile: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
content.topics: Propositional and predicate logic; Truth tables and logical laws; Set theory; Boolean algebra and circuits; Quantifiers; Functions and relations; Proof strategies; Mathematical induction; Recursive definitions; Games without chance and winning strategies; Process modelling
content.methods: Truth-table analysis; Direct proof and proof by cases; Proof by contrapositive and contradiction; Proof with quantifiers; Mathematical induction; Formal process and game modelling

courses.contribution: supplies discrete logic and structures used in algorithm construction and system reasoning
courses.selectedDescription: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.

courses.name: Optimization Methods in AI

content.description2: Covers computational methods for search problems in complex and adversarial environments. Includes uninformed and informed search, local and global search, adversarial games and constraint satisfaction problems.
content.profile: Studies search and optimization for rational agents in known, complex and adversarial environments. Students move from uninformed and heuristic search to local and global optimization, first- and second-order methods and population approaches. Adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimization extend the toolkit. Laboratories and projects require algorithm tracing, implementation and evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.
content.topics: Intelligent and rational agents; Uninformed and informed search; Heuristic functions; Search in complex environments; Local and global optimization; First- and second-order optimization; Population methods; Adversarial games; Constraint satisfaction; Linear programming; Discrete optimization
content.methods: Uninformed and heuristic search; Local and global search; First- and second-order optimization; Population-based optimization; Adversarial search; Monte Carlo tree search; Constraint-satisfaction algorithms; Linear programming; Discrete optimization; Algorithm implementation and experimental evaluation

courses.contribution: implements search, adversarial reasoning and constraint satisfaction for complex-system optimisation
courses.selectedDescription: Optimization Methods in AI studies search and optimisation for rational agents. Topics include uninformed and heuristic search, local and global optimisation, adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimisation. Laboratory exercises and projects develop algorithm implementation, evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.

courses.name: Reinforcement Learning

content.description2: Explores reinforcement learning. Covers theoretical frameworks and algorithms and requires students to implement algorithms and build agents using neural networks that learn through trial and error.

courses.contribution: implements reinforcement-learning algorithms and neural-network agents that learn through trial and error; the description does not establish a physical robot-control application
courses.selectedDescription: Explores reinforcement learning. Covers theoretical frameworks and algorithms and requires students to implement algorithms and build agents using neural networks that learn through trial and error.

courses.name: Algorithms & Data Structures

content.description2: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
content.profile: Studies algorithm design and analysis, emphasizing how algorithms and data structures affect execution time. Students examine sorting, searching, random-number generation, string matching and graph algorithms, then study computability, verification, reductions and complexity classes. Programming and mathematical exercises develop algorithmic understanding, while projects require students to design, execute and report experimental investigations of performance.
content.topics: Abstract data structures; Asymptotic complexity; Random-number generation and sampling; Sorting and stability; String matching and finite automata; Sequential and binary search; Graph traversal; Shortest paths and spanning trees; Topological sorting; Computability and Turing machines; Polynomial-time verification; Reductions and complexity hierarchy
content.methods: Asymptotic time-complexity analysis; Experimental algorithm benchmarking; Algorithm implementation and tracing; Random-number generator testing; Breadth-first and depth-first search; Graph algorithm analysis; Computational reductions

courses.contribution: develops algorithm and data-structure design with performance analysis
courses.selectedDescription: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.

courses.name: Advanced Algorithms

content.description2: Studies modern algebraic algorithms and optimization methods. Emphasises algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling of computational problems.
content.profile: Studies algebraic algorithms and advanced optimization methods through mathematical reasoning, implementation and experimental analysis. Fast and exact arithmetic, number-theoretic algorithms, matrix multiplication and Fourier transformation lead into hashing, greedy methods, dynamic programming and network flows. Laboratories develop algorithmic understanding, while projects investigate exact computing and optimization, including hypotheses, measured performance and sensitivity analysis.
content.topics: Asymptotic time complexity; Fast integer arithmetic; Greatest common divisors and modular arithmetic; Chinese remainder theorem; Arbitrary-precision integers; Primality and factorization; Fast matrix multiplication; Polynomials and Fourier transformation; Hashing and Bloom filters; Greedy algorithms and coding; Dynamic programming; Flow networks; Network science
content.methods: Asymptotic and empirical complexity analysis; Euclidean algorithm; Primality testing and factorization; Fast arithmetic and matrix algorithms; Fast Fourier transformation; Hashing; Greedy optimization; Dynamic programming; Maximum-flow algorithms; Algorithmic experimental design; Sensitivity analysis

courses.contribution: extends mathematical and algebraic algorithms and optimisation for computational system problems
courses.selectedDescription: Studies modern algebraic algorithms and optimization methods. Emphasises algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling of computational problems.

courses.name: Introduction to Data Science

content.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
content.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
content.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
content.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

courses.contribution: provides data cleaning, visualisation and spatial-data analysis for experimental and modelled mechanical-system data
courses.selectedDescription: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

courses.name: Machine Learning

content.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
content.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
content.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
content.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

courses.contribution: applies regression, tree-based and other machine-learning methods to real data
courses.selectedDescription: Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.

courses.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision

content.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
content.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
content.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
content.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images

courses.contribution: studies image feature detection and tracking with documented robotics applications, supporting machine perception without claiming mechanical sensing hardware
courses.selectedDescription: Image Processing & Computer Vision studies how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognise structures and objects. Topics include colour, image statistics, filtering, segmentation, feature detection, tracking and object classification. Practical work uses Python and OpenCV to develop and benchmark an image-recognition pipeline on previously unseen images.

courses.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning

content.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
content.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
content.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
content.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design

courses.contribution: develops neural networks for computer vision and other perception tasks
courses.selectedDescription: Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python, Keras and TensorFlow implementations. Students build and train networks, study backpropagation, regularisation and model evaluation, and apply deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects investigate prediction problems and report experimental results.

courses.name: Robotics

content.description2: Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and manipulation.
content.profile: Studies computational problems in robot motion and manipulation, supported by linear algebra, calculus and geometric modelling. Students analyze forward and inverse kinematics, configuration spaces, collision-free motion planning and grasping, with shorter introductions to sensing and control. Practical work programs a robot arm and gripper; research investigates inverse kinematics for an articulated structure. A smaller component examines a chosen legal, ethical, safety or human-robot issue.
content.topics: Robot architecture and industrial automation; Rotations, orientations and rigid transformations; Forward and inverse kinematics; Trajectory generation; Configuration spaces and obstacles; Exact, approximate and sampling-based motion planning; Collision detection; Sensing and control; Form and force closure; Caging; Non-prehensile manipulation; Social and ethical aspects of robotics
content.methods: Coordinate-frame modelling of articulated structures; Analytic and iterative inverse kinematics; Mathematica computation; Configuration-space modelling; Motion-planning analysis; Collision-detection analysis; Instantaneous-motion and wrench analysis; Robot-arm and gripper programming; Modelling of physical manipulation

courses.contribution: Actual forward/inverse kinematics, collision-free motion planning, grasping/manipulation, robot-arm/gripper programming and a kinematics research investigation directly support robot motion. Sensing/control receive shorter introductions; no mechanical-construction or flexible-robot laboratory equivalence.
courses.selectedDescription: Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and manipulation.

courses.name: Introduction to Programming

content.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
content.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
content.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
content.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

courses.contribution: supplies structured Python programming, testing and debugging for later algorithms and intelligent systems
courses.selectedDescription: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.

courses.name: Mathematical Methods

content.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
content.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
content.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
content.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

courses.contribution: Actual single-variable calculus, complex numbers, differential equations and Mathematica dynamic-model project support physical-system modelling; linear algebra is supplied separately by Linear Algebra.
courses.selectedDescription: Mathematical Methods develops foundational techniques in differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica. A project implements, analyses and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and computational results.

courses.name: Linear Algebra

content.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
content.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
content.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
content.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation

courses.contribution: develops vector spaces, matrices, transformations and eigenvalue methods
courses.selectedDescription: Linear Algebra studies systems of equations, matrices, vectors, linear transformations and vector spaces. Students examine eigenvalues, orthogonality, least-squares approximation, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis, with Mathematica supporting analytical problem-solving.

courses.name: Computational & Numerical Methods

content.description2: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.
content.profile: Develops numerical solutions to mathematical problems that lack convenient analytical solutions, emphasizing when algorithms work and how to validate their output. Students study numerical root finding, interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, ordinary differential equations, and linear and nonlinear systems. Mathematica notebooks apply and compare textbook algorithms with built-in routines, with attention to roundoff, convergence, error, stability and sensitivity.
content.topics: Computer arithmetic and roundoff; Algorithm convergence and error; Scalar root finding; Polynomial interpolation and splines; Parametric curves; Numerical differentiation and integration; Initial-value problems; Multistep and adaptive differential-equation methods; Stability and stiff equations; Linear systems and matrix factorization; Nonlinear systems; Numerical-result validation
content.methods: Mathematica numerical computation; Bisection, fixed-point, Newton and secant methods; Polynomial and spline interpolation; Numerical differentiation and Richardson extrapolation; Simpson, Romberg and Gaussian quadrature; Adaptive quadrature; Euler and Runge-Kutta methods; Multistep predictor-corrector methods; Gaussian elimination and pivoting; Matrix factorizations; Newton and quasi-Newton methods for systems; Steepest descent; Continuation methods

courses.contribution: implements stable numerical solution methods for equations, interpolation, integration and differential equations
courses.selectedDescription: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.

courses.name: Advanced Calculus

content.description2: Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations, including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.

courses.contribution: extends calculus to multiple dimensions, complex-valued functions and differential equations
courses.selectedDescription: Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations, including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.

courses.name: Linear Systems

content.description2: Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing and modelling.
content.profile: Analyzes continuous- and discrete-time signals and linear time-invariant systems through differential or difference equations, impulse responses and frequency-domain representations. Convolution, Fourier series and transforms lead into sampling and reconstruction, filtering, communication systems, Laplace and Z-transforms, and linear feedback. Mathematica laboratories and an applied project connect mathematical properties to signal processing and system behaviour.
content.topics: Continuous- and discrete-time signals; System linearity, causality and stability; Impulse and frequency responses; Convolution; Fourier series and transforms; Time-frequency representations; Sampling, reconstruction and aliasing; Digital filtering; Modulation and multiplexing; Laplace and Z-transforms; Regions of convergence and pole-zero representations; Linear feedback and stability
content.methods: Convolution sums and integrals; Fourier-series and Fourier-transform analysis; Bode-plot analysis; Sampling and signal reconstruction; Filter analysis; Modulation and demodulation; Laplace and Z-transform analysis; Block-diagram system analysis; Root-locus analysis; Mathematica signal and system computation

courses.contribution: Actual continuous/discrete linear systems, convolution, Fourier/Laplace/Z transforms, sampling/filtering and linear-feedback stability with Mathematica laboratories/project support engineering signals/control. No mechanical dynamical modelling or engineering plant laboratory assumed.
courses.selectedDescription: Linear Systems studies signals and linear time-invariant systems. Students examine impulse and frequency responses, convolution, Fourier series and transforms, and the Laplace and Z transforms, including continuous-time and discrete-time representations.

courses.name: Probability & Statistics

content.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
content.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
content.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
content.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

courses.contribution: develops probability, distributions, estimation and simulation for uncertain systems
courses.selectedDescription: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.

courses.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation

content.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
content.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
content.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
content.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations

courses.contribution: Actual solar-panel/e-waste disassembly, metal leaching/recovery, ICP/SEM/EDS analysis and resource-yield experiments support material characterisation and circular products; not precision fabrication or solid-mechanics testing.
courses.selectedDescription: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.

courses.name: Sustainability Essentials I

content.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
content.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
content.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
content.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

courses.contribution: Actual chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles, differential-equation models and iterative biopolymer strength/elasticity laboratory work provide physical foundations and experimental design. Not a full engineering mechanics or thermodynamics sequence.
courses.selectedDescription: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

courses.name: Sustainability Essentials II

content.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
content.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
content.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
content.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

courses.contribution: Actual waves, materials microstructure, stress/strain, Mohr-circle analysis, oscilloscope/spectroscopy and chemistry practicals supply substantive physical/material methods; not specialist solid-mechanics or machining formation.
courses.selectedDescription: Develops physical-science foundations for sustainability through waves, chemistry and materials science. Reflective work and a project apply these topics to analysing greenwashing.

courses.name: Climate Change

content.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
content.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
content.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
content.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

courses.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy

content.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
content.profile: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
content.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning
content.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment

courses.name: Energy & Sustainability

content.description2: Introduces renewable energy resources and technologies, discussing environmental, political and economic constraints. Covers energy storage and demand management and aims to balance energy supply and demand.
content.profile: Studies renewable-energy resources, conversion technologies and their integration into sustainable energy systems. Solar, wind, hydro, geothermal and biomass resources are evaluated through physical principles, resource availability and generation potential. Storage, electricity grids and demand management connect individual technologies to system reliability. Quantitative exercises, a Polysun workshop, short experiments and local mini-grid work develop the ability to assess energy options in practical environmental and economic contexts.
content.topics: Energy demand and renewable resources; Solar radiation and energy yield; Solar thermal and photovoltaic generation; Wind energy; Hydropower; Geothermal energy; Biomass, biogas and biofuels; Electricity grids; Energy storage; Batteries and pumped storage; Smart grids and system integration; Demand management; Mini-grids; Energy-system environmental and economic constraints
content.methods: Renewable-energy resource and yield calculations; Polysun energy-system modelling; Hydropower sizing; Laboratory experimentation on renewable-energy systems; Energy-storage comparison; Mini-grid analysis and design

alignments: Both establish calculus used in quantitative engineering models; UCR also includes matrices and differential equations but is not mechanical-engineering mathematics.
Both use numerical methods to solve engineering-relevant equations; the external course applies them specifically to fluids and solids, which UCR does not reproduce.
Both develop probability and statistical reasoning for quantitative engineering analysis.
Both study signals and linear-system representations; UCR supplies the mathematical system framework without the surrounding mechanical laboratories.
Both include programming and computational problem solving; the external component also teaches mechanical design principles that UCR programming does not reproduce.
Both engage robotic systems; UCR teaches computational kinematics, planning and manipulation, while the external challenge integrates mechanical construction and engineering practice.
Partial ethical-reasoning correspondence through responsibility, privacy, fairness and moral frameworks applied to AI. The engineering-ethics curriculum is broader.

Partial design-project correspondence: customer needs, quantitative product models, production planning and prototypes where feasible. UCR is consumer-product development, not the full advanced mechanical-design project.
Partial physical-mechanics foundation: mechanical principles, material strength and elasticity measurements and modelling. This does not cover the full engineering mechanics course.
Partial materials correspondence through microscopic structure, macroscopic stress/strain, Mohr-circle methods and laboratory observation. Scope and engineering depth differ.

Partial technology-and-society correspondence: climate impacts, justice, energy pathways, stakeholder interviewing and public communication. The ITEC engineering-and-society curriculum has wider purposes.
Both address sustainable energy choices; UCR evaluates renewable-system designs, while the external challenge develops mechanical-engineering decisions around sustainable fuels.

Partial energy-systems correspondence: conversion, storage, resource calculations, experiments and mini-grid design. UCR does not reproduce the complete mechanical energy-storage-and-transport challenge.
